entries.e8432bdb263f757fd11d01808e8f63b7525c70e8: <div sID="gen5925" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="1Sam.31" sID="1Sam.31"/> <div eID="gen5925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5926" type="x-p"/> In the foregoing chapter we had David conquering, yea, more than a conqueror. In this chapter we have Saul conquered and worse than a captive. Providence ordered it that both these things should be doing just at the same time. The very same day; perhaps, that David was triumphing over the Amalekites, were the Philistines triumphing over Saul. One is set over against the other, that men may see what comes of trusting in God and what comes of forsaking him. We left Saul ready to engage the Philistines, with a shaking hand and an aching heart, having had his doom read him from hell, which he would not regard when it was read him from heaven. Let us now see what becomes of him. Here is, I. His army routed, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. His three sons slain, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2">ver. 2</reference>. III. Himself wounded (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">ver. 3</reference>), and slain by his own hand, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.4">ver. 4</reference>. The death of his armour-bearer (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.5">ver. 5</reference>) and all his men, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.6">ver. 6</reference>. IV. His country possessed by the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.7">ver. 7</reference>. His camp plundered, and his dead body deserted, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.8">ver. 8</reference>. His fall triumphed in, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.9">ver. 9</reference>. His body publicly exposed (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.10">ver. 10</reference>) and with difficulty rescued by the men of Jabesh-Gilead, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11-1Sam.31.13">ver. 11-13</reference>. Thus fell the man that was rejected of God.
entries.95f980399bd4dfbdfb97fa19633331138f344c9d: <div eID="gen5926" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of Saul. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5927" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now the Philistines fought against Israel: and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Melchi-shua, Saul's sons. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then said Saul unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him. <hi type="super">6</hi> So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when the men of Israel that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the other side of the valley, and <hi type="italic">they</hi> that <hi type="italic">were</hi> on the other side Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled, and that Saul and his sons were dead, they forsook the cities, and fled; and the Philistines came and dwelt in them. <div eID="gen5927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5928" type="x-p"/> The day of recompence has now come, in which Saul must account for the blood of the Amalekites which he had sinfully spared, and that of the priests which he had more sinfully spilt; that of David too, which he would have spilt, must come into the account. Now his day has come to fall, as David foresaw, when he should descend into battle and perish, <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.10">ch. xxvi. 10</reference>. Come and see the <hi type="italic">righteous judgments of God.</hi> <div eID="gen5928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5929" type="x-p"/> I. He sees his soldiers fall about him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1">v. 1</reference>. Whether the Philistines were more numerous, better posted, and better led on, or what other advantages they had, we are not told; but it seems they were more vigorous, for they made the onset; they fought against Israel, and the Israelites fled and fell. The best of the troops were put into disorder, and multitudes slain, probably those whom Saul had employed in pursuing David. Thus those who had followed him and served him in his sin went before him in his fall and shared with him in his plagues. <div eID="gen5929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5930" type="x-p"/> II. He sees his sons fall before him. The victorious Philistines pressed most forcibly upon the king of Israel and those about him. His three sons were next him, it is probable, and they were all three slain before his face, to his great grief (for they were the hopes of his family) and to his great terror, for they were now the guard of his person, and he could conclude no other than that his own turn would come next. His sons are named (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2">v. 2</reference>), and it grieves us to find Jonathan among them: that wise, valiant, good man, who was as much David's friend as Saul was his enemy, yet falls with the rest. Duty to his father would not permit him to stay at home, or to retire when the armies engaged; and Providence so orders it that he falls in the common fate of his family, though he never involved himself in the guilt of it; so that the observation of Eliphaz does not hold (<reference osisRef="Job.4.7">Job iv. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Who ever perished being innocent?</hi> For here was one. What shall we say to it? 1. God would hereby complete the vexation of Saul in his dying moments, and the judgment that was to be executed upon his house. If the family must fall, Jonathan, that is one of it, must fall with it. 2. He would hereby make David's way to the crown the more clear and open. For, though Jonathan himself would have cheerfully resigned all his title and interest to him (we have no reason to suspect any other), yet it is very probable that many of the people would have made use of his name for the support of the house of Saul, or at least would have come in but slowly to David. If Ish-bosheth (who was now left at home as one unfit for action, and so escaped) had so many friends, what would Jonathan have had, who had been the darling of the people and had never forfeited their favour? Those that were so anxious to have a king like the nations would be zealous for the right line, especially if that threw the crown upon such a head as Jonathan's. This would have embarrassed David; and, if Jonathan could have prevailed to bring in all his interest to David, then it would have been said that Jonathan had made him king, whereas God was to have all the glory. <hi type="italic">This is the Lord's doing.</hi> So that though the death of Jonathan would be a great affliction to David, yet, by making him mindful of his own frailty, as well as by facilitating his accession to the throne, it would be an advantage to him. 3. God would hereby show us that the difference between good and bad is to be made in the other world, not in this. <hi type="italic">All things come alike to all.</hi> We cannot judge of the spiritual or eternal state of any by the manner of their death; for in that <hi type="italic">there is one event to the righteous and to the wicked.</hi> <div eID="gen5930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5931" type="x-p"/> III. He himself is sorely wounded by the Philistines and then slain by his own hand. The archers hit him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3">v. 3</reference>), so that he could neither fight nor fly, and therefore must inevitably fall into their hands. Thus, to make him the more miserable, destruction comes gradually upon him, and he dies so as to feel himself die. To such an extremity was he now reduced that, 1. He was desirous to die by the hand of his own servant rather than by the hand of the Philistines, lest they should abuse him as they had abused Samson. Miserable man! He finds himself dying, and all his care is to keep his body out of the hands of the Philistines, instead of being solicitous to resign his soul into the hands of God who gave it, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Eccl. xii. 7</reference>. As he lived, so he died, proud and jealous, and a terror to himself and all about him. Those who rightly understand the matter think it of small account, in comparison, how it is with them in death, so it may but be well with them after death. Those are in a deplorable condition indeed who, being <hi type="italic">bitter in soul, long for death, but it cometh not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.3.20-Job.3.21">Job iii. 20, 21</reference>), especially those who, despairing of the mercy of God, like Judas, leap into a hell before them, to escape a hell within them. 2. When he could not obtain that favour he became his own executioner, thinking hereby to avoid shame, but running upon a heinous sin, and with it entailing upon his own name a mark of perpetual infamy, as <hi type="italic">felo de se—a self-murderer.</hi> Jonathan, who received his death-wound from the hand of the Philistines and bravely yielded to the fate of war, died on the bed of honour; but Saul died as a fool dieth, as a coward dieth—a proud fool, a sneaking coward; he died as a man that had neither the fear of God nor hope in God, neither the reason of a man nor the religion of an Israelite, much less the dignity of a prince or the resolution of a soldier. Let us all pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, lead us not into temptation,</hi> this temptation. His armour-bearer would not run him through, and he did well to refuse it; for no man's servant ought to be a slave to his master's lusts or passions of any kind. The reason given is that <hi type="italic">he was sorely afraid,</hi> not of death, for he himself ran wilfully upon that immediately; but, having a profound reverence for the king his master, he could not conquer that so far as to do him any hurt; or perhaps he feared lest his trembling hand should give him but half a blow, and so put him to the greater misery. <div eID="gen5931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5932" type="x-p"/> IV. His armour-bearer who refused to kill him refused not to die with him, but <hi type="italic">fell likewise upon his sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.5">v. 5</reference>. This was an aggravating circumstance of the death of Saul, that, by the example of his wickedness in murdering himself, he drew in his servant to be guilty of the same wickedness, and <hi type="italic">perished not alone in his iniquity.</hi> The Jews say that Saul's armour-bearer was Doeg, whom he preferred to that dignity for killing the priests, and, if so, justly does his <hi type="italic">violent dealing return on his own head.</hi> David had foretold concerning him that God would <hi type="italic">destroy him for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.52.5">Ps. lii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen5932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5933" type="x-p"/> V. The country was put into such confusion by the rout of Saul's army that the inhabitants of the neighbouring cities (<hi type="italic">on that side Jordan,</hi> as it might be read) quitted them, and the Philistines, for a time, had possession of them, till things were settled in Israel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.7">v. 7</reference>), to such a sad pass had Saul by his wickedness brought his country, which might have remained in the hands of the uncircumcised if David had not been raised up to repair the breaches of it. See what a king he proved for whom they rejected God and Samuel. They had still done wickedly (it is to be feared) as well as he, and therefore <hi type="italic">were consumed both they and their king,</hi> as the prophet had foretold concerning them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.25">ch. xii. 25</reference>. And to this reference is had long after. <reference osisRef="Hos.13.10-Hos.13.11">Hos. xiii. 10, 11</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Where are thy saviours in all thy cities, of whom thou saidst, Give me a king and princes? I gave thee a king in my anger, and took him away in my wrath;</hi> that is, he was a plague to thee living and dying; thou couldst expect no other."
entries.9b7ab3483a2ccb974cce9b11f51e78665a80f61e: <div eID="gen5933" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Disposal of Saul's Body. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1055.)</title> <div sID="gen5934" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And it came to pass on the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his three sons fallen in mount Gilboa. <hi type="super">9</hi> And they cut off his head, and stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to publish <hi type="italic">it in</hi> the house of their idols, and among the people. <hi type="super">10</hi> And they put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth: and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan. <hi type="super">11</hi> And when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard of that which the Philistines had done to Saul; <hi type="super">12</hi> All the valiant men arose, and went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and came to Jabesh, and burnt them there. <hi type="super">13</hi> And they took their bones, and buried <hi type="italic">them</hi> under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. <div eID="gen5934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5935" type="x-p"/> The scripture makes no mention of the souls of Saul and his sons, what became of them after they were dead (secret things belong not to us), but of their bodies only. <div eID="gen5935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5936" type="x-p"/> I. How they were basely abused by the Philistines. The day after the battle, when they had recovered their fatigue, they came to strip the slain, and, among the rest, found the bodies of Saul and his three sons, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.8">v. 8</reference>. Saul's armour-bearer perhaps intended to honour his master by following the example of his self-murder, and to show thereby how well he loved him; but, if he had consulted his reason more than his passions, he would have spared that foolish compliment, not only in justice to his own life, but in kindness to his master, to whom, by the opportunity of survivorship, he might have done all the service that could be done him by any man after he was dead; for he might, in the night, have conveyed away his body, and those of his sons, and buried them decently. But such false and foolish notions these vain men have (though they would be wise) of giving and receiving honour. Nay, it should seem, Saul might have saved himself the fatal thrust and have made his escape: for the pursuers (in fear of whom he slew himself) came not to the place where he was till the next day. But whom God will destroy he infatuates and utterly <hi type="italic">consumes with his terrors.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Job.18.5-Job.18.21">Job xviii. 5</reference>, &c. Finding Saul's body (which now that it lay extended on the bloody turf was distinguishable from the rest by its length, as it was, while erect, by its height, when he proudly overlooked the surrounding crowd), they will, in that, triumph over Israel's crown, and meanly gratify a barbarous and brutish revenge by insulting the deserted corpse, which, when alive, they had stood in awe of. 1. They cut off his head. Had they designed in this to revenge the cutting off of Goliath's head they would rather have cut off the head of David, who did that execution, when he was in their country. They intended it, in general, for a reproach to Israel, who promised themselves that a crowned and an anointed head would save them from the Philistines, and a particular reproach to Saul, who was taller by the head than other men (which perhaps he was wont to boast of), but was now shorter by the head. 2. They stripped him of his armour (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.9">v. 9</reference>), and sent that to be set up as a trophy of their victory, in the house of Ashtaroth their goddess (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.10">v. 10</reference>); and we are told, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.10">1 Chron. x. 10</reference> (though it is omitted here), that they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. Thus did they ascribe the honour of their victory, not as they ought to have done to the real justice of the true God, but to the imaginary power of their false gods, and by this respect paid to pretended deities shame those who give not the praise of their achievements to the living God. Ashtaroth, the idol that Israel had many a time gone a whoring after, now triumphs over them. 3. They sent expresses throughout their country, and ordered public notice to be given in the houses of their gods of the victory they had obtained (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.9">v. 9</reference>), that public rejoicings might be made and thanks given to their gods. This David regretted sorely, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.20">2 Sam. i. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Tell it not in Gath.</hi> 4. They fastened his body and the bodies of his sons (as appears, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">v. 12</reference>) to the wall of <hi type="italic">Beth-shan,</hi> a city that lay not far from Gilboa and very near to the river Jordan. Hither the dead bodies were dragged and here hung up in chains, to be devoured by the birds of prey. Saul slew himself to avoid being abused by the Philistines, and never was royal corpse so abused as his was, perhaps the more if they understood that he slew himself for that reason. He that thinks to save his honour by sin will certainly lose it. See to what a height of insolence the Philistines had arrived just before David was raised up, who perfectly subdued them. Now that they had slain Saul and his sons they thought the land of Israel was their own for ever, but they soon found themselves deceived. When God has accomplished his whole work by them he will accomplish it upon them. See <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6-Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen5936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5937" type="x-p"/> II. How they were bravely rescued by the men of Jabesh-Gilead. Little more than the river Jordan lay between Beth-shan and Jabesh-Gilead, and Jordan was in that place passable by its fords; a bold adventure was therefore made by the valiant men of that city, who in the night passed the river, took down the dead bodies, and gave them decent burial, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11">v. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.13">13</reference>. This they did, 1. Out of a common concern for the honour of Israel, or the land of Israel, which ought not to be defiled by the exposing of any dead bodies, and especially of the crown of Israel, which was thus profaned by the uncircumcised. 2. Out of a particular sense of gratitude to Saul, for his zeal and forwardness to rescue them from the Ammonites when he first came to the throne, <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.27">ch. xi.</reference> It is an evidence of a generous spirit and an encouragement to beneficence when the remembrance of kindnesses is thus retained, and they are thus returned in an extremity. The men of Jabesh-Gilead would have done Saul better service if they had sent their valiant men to him sooner, to strengthen him against the Philistines. But his day had come to fall, and now this is all the service they can do him, in honour to his memory. We find not that any general mourning was made for the death of Saul, as was for the death of Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.1">ch. xxv. 1</reference>), only those Gileadites of Jabesh did him honour at his death; for, (1.) They made a burning for the bodies, to perfume them. So some understand the burning of them. They burnt spices over them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">v. 12</reference>. And that it was usual thus to do honour to their deceased friends, at least their princes, appears by the account of Asa's funeral (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2 Chron. xvi. 14</reference>), that <hi type="italic">they made a very great burning for him.</hi> Or (as some think) they burnt the flesh, because it began to putrefy. (2.) They buried the bodies, when, by burning over them, they had sweetened them (or, if they burnt them, they buried the bones and ashes), under a tree, which served for a grave-stone and monument. And, (3.) They <hi type="italic">fasted seven days,</hi> that is, each day of the seven they fasted till the evening; thus they lamented the death of Saul and the present distracted state of Israel, and perhaps joined prayers with their fasting for the re-establishment of their shattered state. Though, <hi type="italic">when the wicked perish there is shouting</hi> (that is, it is to be hoped a better state of things will ensue, which will be matter of joy), yet humanity obliges us to show a decent respect to dead bodies, especially those of princes. <div eID="gen5937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5938" type="x-p"/> This book began with the birth of Samuel, but now it ends with the burial of Saul, the comparing of which two together will teach us to prefer the honour that comes from God before any of the honours which this world pretends to have the disposal of.  <chapter eID="1Sam.31"/> <div eID="gen5938" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5204" osisID="1Sam" type="book"/>

entries.55f7de168135bbee95986b9edce74b49bfa7e824: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2817"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <div sID="gen3863" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.7">1Sa 31:1-7</reference>. Saul Having Lost His Army at Gilboa, and His Sons Being Slain, He and His Armor-bearer Kill Themselves.<div eID="gen3863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2817"/><hi type="bold">1. Now the Philistines fought against Israel--</hi>In a regular engagement, in which the two armies met (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1-1Sam.28.4">1Sa 28:1-4</reference>), the Israelites were forced to give way, being annoyed by the arrows of the enemy, which, destroying them at a distance before they came to close combat, threw them into panic and disorder. Taking advantage of the heights of Mount Gilboa, [the Israelites] attempted to rally, but in vain. Saul and his sons fought like heroes; but the onset of the Philistines being at length mainly directed against the quarter where they were, Jonathan and two brothers, Abinadab or Ishui (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49">1Sa 14:49</reference>) and Melchishua, overpowered by numbers, were killed on the spot. <div eID="gen3864" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e8e98fc0efe570653389da3f288f8968df986e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2818"/><div sID="gen3865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2818"/><hi type="bold">3-5. the battle went sore against Saul, &c.--</hi>He seems to have bravely maintained his ground for some time longer; but exhausted with fatigue and loss of blood, and dreading that if he fell alive into the enemy's hands, they would insolently maltreat him (<reference osisRef="Josh.8.29">Jos 8:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.8.21">Jud 8:21</reference>), he requested his armor bearer to despatch him. However, that officer refused to do so. Saul then falling on the point of his sword killed himself; and the armor bearer, who, according to Jewish writers, was Doeg, following the example of his master, put an end to his life also. They died by one and the same sword--the very weapon with which they had massacred the Lord's servants at Nob. <div eID="gen3865" type="x-p"/>
entries.3381ca56510e87cd31917e9160bd259981933a9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2819"/><div sID="gen3866" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2819"/><hi type="bold">6. So Saul died--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.13">1Ch 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.11">Ho 13:11</reference>).<div eID="gen3866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and his three sons--</hi>The influence of a directing Providence is evidently to be traced in permitting the death of Saul's three eldest and most energetic sons, particularly that of Jonathan, for whom, had he survived his father, a strong party would undoubtedly have risen and thus obstructed the path of David to the throne.<div eID="gen3867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and all his men, that same day together--</hi>his servants or bodyguard (<reference osisRef="1Chr.10.6">1Ch 10:6</reference>). <div eID="gen3868" type="x-p"/>
entries.24832b63890737f45c34325a690f21f685322d2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2820"/><div sID="gen3869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2820"/><hi type="bold">7. the men of Israel that were on the other side of the valley--</hi>probably the valley of Jezreel--the largest and southernmost of the valleys that run between Little Hermon and the ridges of the Gilboa range direct into the Jordan valley. It was very natural for the people in the towns and villages there to take fright and flee, for had they waited the arrival of the victors, they must, according to the war usages of the time, have been deprived either of their liberty or their lives.<div eID="gen3869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3870" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.8-1Sam.31.10">1Sa 31:8-10</reference>. The Philistines Triumph over Their Dead Bodies. <div eID="gen3870" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd4f5ef023adf54b67b80777fe4e8a572fbf08b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2821"/><div sID="gen3871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2821"/><hi type="bold">8-9. on the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, that they found Saul and his three sons fallen--</hi>On discovering the corpses of the slaughtered princes on the battlefield, the enemy reserved them for special indignities. They consecrated the armor of the king and his sons to the temple of Ashtaroth fastened their bodies on the temple of Shen, while they fixed the royal heads ignominiously in the temple of Dagon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.10.10">1Ch 10:10</reference>); thus dividing the glory among their several deities. <div eID="gen3871" type="x-p"/>
entries.55106730dca88665e41f5fb8d7c755abe2dab774: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2822"/><div sID="gen3872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2822"/><hi type="bold">10. to the wall--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Sam.21.12">2Sa 21:12</reference>)--"the street" of Beth-shan. The street was called from the temple which stood in it. And they had to go along it to the wall of the city (see <reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>).<div eID="gen3872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3873" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11-1Sam.31.13">1Sa 31:11-13</reference>. The Men of Jabesh-gilead Recover the Bodies and Bury Them at Jabesh. <div eID="gen3873" type="x-p"/>
entries.859c0088e518aa75af88413f0a12805c01165bd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2823"/><div sID="gen3874" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2823"/><hi type="bold">11-13. the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard of that which the Philistines had done--</hi>Mindful of the important and timely services Saul had rendered them, they gratefully and heroically resolved not to suffer such indignities to be inflicted on the remains of the royal family. <div eID="gen3874" type="x-p"/>

entries.efe6fa488192acb01120606b3cc47bc523d52e7c: <div eID="gen10610" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10611" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10612" type="x-p"/> A battle in Mount Gilboa between Israel and the Philistines; in which the former are defeated, and Saul's three sons slain, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1">1Sam 31:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2">1Sam 31:2</reference>. Saul, being mortally wounded, and afraid to fall alive into the hands of the Philistines, desires his armor-bearer to despatch him; which he refusing, Saul falls on his sword, and his armor-bearer does the same, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.3-1Sam.31.6">1Sam 31:3-6</reference>. The Israelites on the other side of the valley forsake their cities, and the Philistines come and dwell in them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.7">1Sam 31:7</reference>. The Philistines, finding Saul and his three sons among the slain, strip them of their armor, which they put in the house of Ashtaroth, cut of their heads, send the news to all the houses of their idols, and fasten the bodies of Saul and his three sons to the walls of Beth-shan, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.8-1Sam.31.10">1Sam 31:8-10</reference>. Valiant men of Jabesh-gilead go by night, and take away the bodies; burn them at Jabesh; bury their bones under a tree; and fast seven days, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11-1Sam.31.13">1Sam 31:11-13</reference>. <div eID="gen10612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10613" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10614" type="x-p"/> Now the Philistines fought - This is the continuation of the account given in <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1-1Sam.29.11">1Sam 29:1-11</reference>. <div eID="gen10614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10615" type="x-p"/> The men of Israel fled - It seems as if they were thrown into confusion at the first onset, and turned their backs upon their enemies.
entries.b822e0f4647c104b9f4888546f3974e671f85393: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10616" type="x-p"/> Followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons - They, seeing the discomfiture of their troops, were determined to sell their lives as dear as possible, and therefore maintained the battle till the three brothers were slain.
entries.c981daf02e297db702e9e3a3d8572ef973ee3e59: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10617" type="x-p"/> He was sore wounded of the archers - It is likely that Saul's sons were slain by the archers, and that Saul was now mortally wounded by the same. Houbigant translates, The archers rushed upon him, from whom he received a grievous wound. He farther remarks that had not Saul been grievously wounded, and beyond hope of recovery, he would not have wished his armor-bearer to despatch him; as he might have continued still to fight, or have made his escape from this most disastrous battle. Some of the versions render it, He Feared the archers greatly; but this is by no means likely.
entries.cd0b4d50897c7dd2723af3e04f4054ef837c934f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10618" type="x-p"/> Draw thy sword, and thrust me through - Dr. Delaney has some good observations on this part of the subject: "Saul and his armor-bearer died by the same sword. That his armor-bearer died by his own sword is out of all doubt; the text expressly tells us so; and that Saul perished by the same sword is sufficiently evident. Draw Thy sword, says he to him, and thrust me through; which, when he refused, Saul, says the text, took The sword, (את החרב eth hachereb, the very sword), and fell upon it. What sword? Not his own, for then the text would have said so; but, in the plain natural grammatical construction, the sword before mentioned must be the sword now referred to, that is, his armor-bearer's, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.4">1Chr 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.5">1Chr 10:5</reference>. Now it is the established tradition of all the Jewish nation that this armor-bearer was Doeg, and I see no reason why it should be discredited; and if so, then Saul and his executioner both fell by that weapon with which they had before massacred the priests of God. So Brutus and Cassius killed themselves with the same swords with which they stabbed Caesar; and Calippus was stabbed with the same sword with which he stabbed Dio."
entries.4bf08096b7b340343b68bfa342ac94ff7d44fe7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10619" type="x-p"/> And all his men - Probably meaning those of his troops which were his life or body guards: as to the bulk of the army, it fled at the commencement of the battle, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1">1Sam 31:1</reference>.
entries.b97d1dc550ca91e808a608a6bd350d343e4a16a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10620" type="x-p"/> The men of Israel that were on the other side of the valley - They appear to have been panic-struck, and therefore fled as far as they could out of the reach of the Philistines. As the Philistines possessed Beth-shan, situated near to Jordan, the people on the other side of that river, fearing for their safety, fled also.
entries.77836746a276439480c9cacab027383af56f9710: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10621" type="x-p"/> On the morrow - It is very likely that the battle and pursuit continued till the night, so that there was no time till the next day to strip and plunder the slain.
entries.b2d2db1778e2526f3121f99f9c35a20ea3de4807: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10622" type="x-p"/> And they cut off his head - It is possible that they cut off the heads of his three sons likewise; for although only his head is said to be cut off, and his body only to be fastened to the walls of Beth-shan, yet we find that the men of Jabesh-gilead found both his body and the bodies of his three sons, fastened to the walls, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">1Sam 31:12</reference>. <div eID="gen10622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10623" type="x-p"/> Perhaps they only took off Saul's head, which they sent about to their temples as a trophy of their victory, when they sent the news of the defeat of the Israelites through all their coasts, and at last placed it in the temple of Dagon, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.10">1Chr 10:10</reference>.
entries.26e50220902dc0fc065ec6fcbea026892350ea75: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen10623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10624" type="x-p"/> They put his armor in the house of Ashtaroth - As David had done in placing the sword of Goliath in the tabernacle. We have already seen that it was common for the conquerors to consecrate armor and spoils taken in war, to those who were the objects of religious worship. <div eID="gen10624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10625" type="x-p"/> They fastened his body to the wall - Probably by means of iron hooks; but it is said, <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.12">2Sam 21:12</reference>, that these bodies were fastened in the Street of Beth-shan. This may mean that the place where they were fastened to the wall was the main street or entrance into the city.
entries.142303029769d6dacee4effd1f43653110e637eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10626" type="x-p"/> When the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard - This act of the men of Jabesh-gilead was an act of gratitude due to Saul, who, at the very commencement of his reign, rescued them from Nahash, king of the Ammonites, (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1">1Sam 11:1</reference>, etc.), and by his timely succours saved them from the deepest degradation and the most oppressive tyranny. This heroic act, with the seven days' fast, showed that they retained a due sense of their obligation to this unfortunate monarch.
entries.4df775f7a342a57497ebce27a85df180eff85a60: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen10626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> And burnt them there - It has been denied that the Hebrews burnt the bodies of the dead, but that they buried them in the earth, or embalmed them, and often burnt spices around them, etc. These no doubt were the common forms of sepulture, but neither of these could be conveniently practiced in the present case. They could not have buried them about Beth-shan without being discovered; and as to embalming, that was most likely out of all question, as doubtless the bodies were now too putrid to bear it. They therefore burnt them, because there was no other way of disposing of them at that time so as to do them honor; and the bones and ashes they collected, and buried under a tree or in a grove at Jabesh.
entries.008bcdd4372a7bfd7c9f3603fed46bfc5adedf2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10628" type="x-p"/> And fasted seven days - To testify their sincere regret for his unfortunate death, and the public calamity that had fallen upon the land. <div eID="gen10628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10629" type="x-p"/> Thus ends the troublesome, and I had almost said the useless, reign of Saul. A king was chosen in opposition to the will of the Most High; and the government of God in effect rejected, to make way for this king. <div eID="gen10629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10630" type="x-p"/> Saul was at first a very humble young man, and conducted himself with great propriety; but his elevation made him proud, and he soon became tyrannical in his private conduct and in his political measures. His natural temper was not good; he was peevish, fretful, and often outrageous; and these bad dispositions, unchecked by proper application to the grace of God, became every day more headstrong and dangerous. Through their violence he seems at times to have been wholly carried away and deranged; and this derangement appears to have been occasionally greatly exacerbated by diabolical influences. This led him to take his friends for his foes; so that in his paroxysms he strove to imbrue his hands in their blood, and more than once attempted to assassinate his own son; and most causelessly and inhumanly ordered the innocent priests of the Lord at Nob to be murdered. This was the worst act in his whole life. <div eID="gen10630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> Saul was but ill qualified for a proper discharge of the regal functions. The reader will remember that he was chosen rather as a general of the armies than as civil governor. The administration of the affairs of the state was left chiefly to Samuel, and Saul led forth the armies to battle. <div eID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10632" type="x-p"/> As a general he gave proof of considerable capacity; he was courageous, prompt, decisive, and persevering; and, except in the last unfortunate battle in which he lost his life, generally led his troops to victory. <div eID="gen10632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10633" type="x-p"/> Saul was a weak man, and very capricious; this is amply proved by his unreasonable jealousy against David, and his continual suspicion that all were leagued against him. It is also evident, in his foolish adjuration relative to the matter of the honey (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24-1Sam.14.30">1Sam 14:24-30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38-1Sam.14.44">1Sam 14:38-44</reference>) in which, to save his rash and nonsensical oath, he would have sacrificed Jonathan his son! <div eID="gen10633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10634" type="x-p"/> The question, "Was Saul a good king?" has already in effect been answered. He was on the whole a good man, as far as we know, in private life; but he was a bad king; for he endeavored to reign independently of the Jewish constitution; he in effect assumed the sacerdotal office and functions, and thus even changed what was essential to that constitution. He not only offered sacrifices which belonged to the priests alone; but in the most positive manner went opposite to the orders of that God whose vicegerent he was. <div eID="gen10634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10635" type="x-p"/> Of his conduct in visiting the woman at En-dor I have already given my opinion, and to this I must refer. His desperate circumstances imposed on the weakness of his mind; and he did in that instance an act which, in his jurisprudential capacity, he had disapproved by the edict which banished all witches, etc., from Israel. Yet in this act he only wished to avail himself of the counsel and advice of his friend Samuel. <div eID="gen10635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> To the question, "Was not Saul a self-murderer?" I scruple not to answer, "No." He was to all appearance mortally wounded, when he begged his armor-bearer to extinguish the remaining spark of life; and he was afraid that the Philistines might abuse his body, if they found him alive; and we can scarcely say how much of indignity is implied in this word; and his falling on his sword was a fit of desperation, which doubtless was the issue of a mind greatly agitated, and full of distraction. A few minutes longer, and his life would in all probability have ebbed out; but though this wound accelerated his death, yet it could not be properly the cause of it, as he was mortally wounded before, and did it on the conviction that he could not survive. <div eID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> Taking Saul's state and circumstances together, I believe there is not a coroner's inquest in this nation that would not have brought in a verdict of derangement; while the pious and the humane would everywhere have consoled themselves with the hope that God had extended mercy to his soul. <div eID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10638" type="x-p"/> Millbrook, June 11, 1818. <div eID="gen10638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10639" type="x-p"/> Ended this examination August 13, 1827. - A.C.  <chapter eID="1Sam.31"/> <div eID="gen10639" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen9431" osisID="1Sam" type="book"/>

entries.bc337cc982c4cafc458bd8027c74594f95536267: <div eID="gen4195" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Death and Burial of Saul and His Sons - <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.13">1Sa 31:1-13</reference></title> <div sID="gen4196" type="x-p"/> The end of the unhappy king corresponded to his life ever since the day of his rejection as king. When he had lost the battle, and saw his three sons fallen at his side, and the archers of the enemy pressing hard upon him, without either repentance or remorse he put an end to his life by suicide, to escape the disgrace of being wounded and abused by the foe (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.7">1Sa 31:1-7</reference>). But he did not attain his object; for the next day the enemy found his corpse and those of his sons, and proceeded to plunder, mutilate, and abuse them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.8-1Sam.31.10">1Sa 31:8-10</reference>). However, the king of Israel was not to be left to perish in utter disgrace. The citizens of Jabesh remembered the deliverance which Saul had brought to their city after his election as king, and showed their gratitude by giving an honourable burial to Saul and his sons (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11-1Sam.31.13">1Sa 31:11-13</reference>). There is a parallel to this chapter in <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.1-1Chr.10.14">1Ch 10:1-14</reference>, which agrees exactly with the account before us, with very few deviations indeed, and those mostly verbal, and merely introduces a hortatory clause at the end (<reference osisRef="1Chr.10.13">1Ch 10:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.14">1Ch 10:14</reference>). <div eID="gen4196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4197" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1">1Sa 31:1</reference> <div eID="gen4197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4198" type="x-p"/> The account of the war between the Philistines and Israel, the commencement of which has already been mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.1">1Sa 28:1</reference>, 1Sa 28:4., and <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>, is resumed in <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.1">1Sa 31:1</reference> in a circumstantial clause; and to this there is attached a description of the progress and result of the battle, more especially with reference to Saul. Consequently, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.1">1Ch 10:1</reference>, where there had been no previous allusion to the war, the participle נלחמים is changed into the perfect. The following is the way in which we should express the circumstantial clause: “Now when the Philistines were fighting against Israel, the men of Israel fled before the Philistines, and slain men fell in the mountains of Gilboa” (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.4">1Sa 28:4</reference>). The principal engagement took place in the plain of Jezreel. But when the Israelites were obliged to yield, they fled up the mountains of Gilboa, and were pursued and slain there.
entries.361545bf432ed2b1ecbae422afd08908c4641965: <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.2-1Sam.31.6">1Sa 31:2-6</reference> <div eID="gen4198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4199" type="x-p"/> The Philistines followed Saul, smote (i.e., put to death) his three sons (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.49">1Sa 14:49</reference>), and fought fiercely against Saul himself. <hi type="italic">When the archers</hi> (בּקּשׁת אנשׁים is an explanatory apposition to המּורים) <hi type="italic">hit him</hi>, i.e., overtook him, <hi type="italic">he was greatly alarmed at them</hi> (יחל, from חיל or חוּל),<note placement="foot">The lxx have adopted the rendering καὶ ἐτραυμάτισαν εἰς τὰ ὑποχόνδρια, they wounded him in the abdomen, whilst the Vulgate rendering is <hi type="italic">vulneratus est vehementer a sagittariis</hi>. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.3">1Ch 10:3</reference> the <hi type="italic">Sept.</hi> rendering is καὶ ἐπόνεσεν ἀπὸ τῶν τόξων, and that of the Vulgate <hi type="italic">et vulneraverunt jaculis</hi>. The translators have therefore derived יחל from חלל = חלה, and then given a free rendering to the other words. But this rendering is overthrown by the word מאד, very, vehemently, to say nothing of the fact that the verb חלל or חלה cannot be proved to be ever used in the sense of wounding. If Saul had been so severely wounded that he could not kill himself, and therefore asked his armour-bearer to slay him, as Thenius supposes, he would not have had the strength to pierce himself with his sword when the armour-bearer refused. The further conjecture of Thenius, that the Hebrew text should be read thus, in accordance with the lxx, המּררים אל ויּחל, “he was wounded in the region of the gall,” is opposed by the circumstance that ὑποχόνδρια is not the gall or region of the gall, but what is under the χόνδρος, or breast cartilage, viz., the abdomen and bowels.</note> and called upon his armour-bearer to pierce him with the sword, “<hi type="italic">lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and play with me</hi>,” i.e., cool their courage upon me by maltreating me. But as the armour-bearer would not do this, because he was very much afraid, since he was supposed to be answerable for the king’s life, Saul inflicted death upon himself with his sword; whereupon the armour-bearer also fell upon his sword and died with his king, so that on that day Saul and this three sons and his armour-bearer all died; also “<hi type="italic">all his men</hi>” (for which we have “all his house” in the Chronicles), i.e., not all the warriors who went out with him to battle, but all the king’s servants, or all the members of his house, sc., who had taken part in the battle. Neither Abner nor his son Ishbosheth was included, for the latter was not in the battle; and although the former was Saul’s cousin and commander-in-chief (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.50-1Sam.14.51">1Sa 14:50-51</reference>), he did not belong to his house or servants.
entries.0107caa4f2145003c03061a2f95a8c34f37a909b: <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.7">1Sa 31:7</reference> <div eID="gen4199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4200" type="x-p"/> When the men of Israel upon the sides that were opposite to the valley (Jezreel) and the Jordan saw that the Israelites (the Israelitish troop) fled, and Saul and his sons were dead, they took to flight out of the cities, whereupon the Philistines took possession of them. עבר is used here to signify the side opposite to the place of conflict in the valley of Jezreel, which the writer assumed as his standpoint (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.40">1Sa 14:40</reference>); so that העמק עבר is the country to the west of the valley of Jezreel, and היּרדּן עבר the country to the west of the Jordan, i.e., between Gilboa and the Jordan. These districts, i.e., the whole of the country round about the valley of Jezreel, the Philistines took possession of, so that the whole of the northern part of the land of Israel, in other words the whole land with the exception of Peraea and the tribe-land of Judah, came into their hands when Saul was slain.
entries.2ad6ab095ddaeb853fe40fe13140c088efab945e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.8-1Sam.31.10">1Sa 31:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen4200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4201" type="x-p"/> On the day following the battle, when the Philistines tripped the slain, they found Saul and his three sons lying upon Gilboa; and having cut off their heads and plundered their weapons, they went them (the heads and weapons) as trophies into the land of the Philistines, i.e., round about to the different towns and hamlets of their land, to announce the joyful news in their idol-temples (the writer of the Chronicles mentions the idols themselves) and to the people, and then deposited their weapons (the weapons of Saul and his sons) in the Astarte-houses. But the corpses they fastened to the town-wall of Beth-shean, i.e., Beisan, in the valley of the Jordan (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>). <hi type="italic">Beth-azabbim</hi> and <hi type="italic">Beth-ashtaroth</hi> are composite words; the first part is indeclinable, and the plural form is expressed by the second word: <hi type="italic">idol-houses</hi> and <hi type="italic">Astarte-houses</hi>, like <hi type="italic">beth-aboth</hi> (father's-houses: see at <reference osisRef="Exod.6.14">Exo 6:14</reference>). On the <hi type="italic">Astartes</hi>, see at Jdg 2:13. It is not expressly stated indeed in <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.9">1Sa 31:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.10">1Sa 31:10</reference>, that the Philistines plundered the bodies of Saul’s sons as well, and mutilated them by cutting off their heads; but ראשׁו and כּליו, <hi type="italic">his</hi> (i.e., Saul’s) <hi type="italic">head</hi> and <hi type="italic">his weapons</hi>, alone are mentioned. At the same time, it is every evident from <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">1Sa 31:12</reference>, where the Jabeshites are said to have taken down from the wall of Beth-shean not Saul’s body only, but the bodies of his sons also, that the Philistines had treated the corpses of Saul’s sons in just the same manner as that of Saul himself. The writer speaks distinctly of the abuse of Saul’s body only, because it was his death that he had chiefly in mind at the time. To the word וישׁלּחוּ we must supply in thought the object ראשׁו and כּליו from the preceding clause. גּויּת and גּויּת (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.10">1Sa 31:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">1Sa 31:12</reference>) are the corpses without the heads. The fact that the Philistines nailed them to the town-wall of Beth-shean presupposes the capture of that city, from which it is evident that they had occupied the land as far as the Jordan. The definite word <hi type="italic">Beth-ashtaroth</hi> is changed by the writer of the Chronicles into <hi type="italic">Beth-elohim</hi>, temples of the gods; or rather he has interpreted it in this manner without altering the sense, as the Astartes are merely mentioned as the principal deities for the idols generally. The writer of the Chronicles has also omitted to mention the nailing of the corpses to the wall of Beth-shean, but he states instead that “they fastened his skull in the temple of Dagon,” a fact which is passed over in the account before us. From this we may see how both writers have restricted themselves to the principal points, or those which appeared to them of the greatest importance (vid., Bertheau on <reference osisRef="1Chr.10.10">1Ch 10:10</reference>).
entries.48e90e2d860fc870b35f3430393bb8227b13e5de: <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11-1Sam.31.13">1Sa 31:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen4201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4202" type="x-p"/> When the inhabitants of Jabesh in Gilead heard this, all the brave men of the town set out to Beth-shean, took down the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there. “<hi type="italic">But their bones they buried under the tamarisk at Jabesh, and fasted seven days</hi>,” to mourn for the king their former deliverer (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:1-15</reference>). These statements are given in a very condensed form in the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="1Sam.31.11">1Sa 31:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.12">1Sa 31:12</reference>). Not only is the fact that “they went the whole night” omitted, as being of no essential importance to the general history; but the removal of the bodies from the town-wall is also passed over, because their being fastened there had not been mentioned, and also the burning of the bodies. The reason for the last omission is not to be sought for in the fact that the author of the Chronicles regarded burning as ignominious, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.20.14">Lev 20:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.21.9">Lev 21:9</reference>, but because he did not see how to reconcile the burning of the bodies with the burial of the bones. It was not the custom in Israel to burn the corpse, but to bury it in the ground. The former was restricted to the worst criminals (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.20.14">Lev 20:14</reference>). Consequently the Chaldee interpreted the word “burnt” as relating to the burning of spices, a custom which we meet with afterwards as a special honour shown to certain of the kings of Judah on the occasion of their burial (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.19">2Ch 21:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">Jer 34:5</reference>). But this is expressed by שׂרפה לו שׂרף, “to make a burning for him,” whereas here it is stated distinctly that “they burnt them.” The reason for the burning of the bodies in the case of Saul and his sons is to be sought for in the peculiarity of the circumstances; viz., partly in the fact that the bodies were mutilated by the removal of the heads, and therefore a regular burial of the dead was impossible, and partly in their anxiety lest, if the Philistines followed up their victory and came to Jabesh, they should desecrate the bodies still further. But even this was not a complete burning to ashes, but merely a burning of the skin and flesh; so that the bones still remained, and they were buried in the ground under a shady tree. Instead of “under the (well-known) tamarisk” (<hi type="italic">eshel</hi>), we have האלה תּחת (under the strong tree) in 1Ch 10:11. David afterwards had them fetched away and buried in Saul’s family grave at Zela, in the land of Benjamin (2Sa 21:11.). The seven days’ fast kept by the Jabeshites was a sign of public and general mourning on the part of the inhabitants of that town at the death of the king, who had once rescued them from the most abominable slavery. <div eID="gen4202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4203" type="x-p"/> In this ignominious fate of Saul there was manifested the righteous judgment of God in consequence of the hardening of his heart. But the love which the citizens of Jabesh displayed in their treatment of the corpses of Saul and his sons, had reference not to the king as rejected by God, but to the king as anointed with the Spirit of Jehovah, and was a practical condemnation, not of the divine judgment which had fallen upon Saul, but of the cruelty of the enemies of Israel and its anointed. For although Saul had waged war almost incessantly against the Philistines, it is not known that in any one of his victories he had ever been guilty of such cruelties towards the conquered and slaughtered foe as could justify this barbarous revenge on the part of the uncircumcised upon his lifeless corpse.  <chapter eID="1Sam.31"/> <div eID="gen4203" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen3614" osisID="1Sam" type="book"/>
